mcqs.question: What's the fundamental difference between push-based CD and pull-based GitOps?
options: GitOps doesn't use version control at all, unlike push-based CD
In push-based CD the pipeline holds cluster-write credentials and pushes changes in; in GitOps an in-cluster agent pulls desired state from git and applies it itself
Push-based CD is always faster because it skips the git diff step
GitOps requires a service mesh while push-based CD does not
mcqs.explanation: The defining distinction is who initiates the change and who holds credentials: push-based CD needs an external pipeline with cluster-write access, while GitOps flips it so an in-cluster agent pulls and applies, needing only read access to git.

mcqs.question: In the GitOps reconciliation loop, what happens if the agent detects the cluster's actual state no longer matches git?
options: It updates the git repo to match whatever the cluster is currently running
It pauses all deployments until a human manually resolves the difference
It applies whatever changes are needed to converge the cluster back to the state declared in git
It deletes the mismatched resources and waits for someone to recreate them
mcqs.explanation: The loop always converges toward git as the source of truth — it applies changes to make the cluster match git, not the reverse. It doesn't silently rewrite git to match cluster drift, and it doesn't require a human pause for routine convergence.

mcqs.question: A team adopts Argo CD but their CI pipeline still holds a cluster-admin kubeconfig and runs `kubectl apply` directly for some changes. What's the risk?
options: This is actually the recommended hybrid pattern for large clusters
There's no risk, since Argo CD will simply overwrite whatever the pipeline applies
The risk is purely about deploy speed, not security
It creates two competing paths to change the cluster and means compromising the pipeline still grants full cluster-write access, defeating GitOps's core security benefit
mcqs.explanation: GitOps's security value comes specifically from credentials flowing one way -- in from the cluster, never held externally. Keeping a pipeline with standing cluster-admin access reintroduces exactly the attack surface GitOps is meant to remove, regardless of Argo CD also being present.

mcqs.question: Why doesn't committing a Kubernetes `Secret` manifest directly to the GitOps repo work as a secrets strategy?
options: The plaintext secret value lives in git history forever, so anyone with repo read access -- and anyone who ever had it -- can read the value, regardless of later deleting the file
Kubernetes rejects Secret manifests that arrive via GitOps sync
Argo CD and Flux automatically strip Secret resources before applying them
It works fine as long as the repo is private
mcqs.explanation: A private repo doesn't fix the core problem: git history is permanent, so a plaintext secret committed once stays recoverable from history even after later removal or repo access changes. Sealed Secrets or an External Secrets Operator avoid ever putting plaintext in git at all.

mcqs.question: An on-call engineer makes a manual `kubectl edit` to stop an active incident, but the GitOps agent reverts it a few minutes later at the next reconciliation. What should they have done instead?
options: Explicitly pause auto-sync before making the manual change, then resume sync and commit the real fix to git once stable
Nothing differently -- self-healing reverting an emergency fix is an unavoidable cost of GitOps
Delete the GitOps agent entirely until the incident is resolved
Make the same manual edit repeatedly until it happens to survive a reconciliation cycle
mcqs.explanation: Both Argo CD and Flux support pausing auto-sync precisely for this situation -- it lets a manual emergency fix stand without racing the next reconciliation, and normal git-driven sync resumes once the real fix is committed. Repeatedly re-applying a change or removing the agent are not the supported mechanisms.
